Abstract 
The development of chassis active safety control technology has improved vehicle stability under extreme condi-
tions. However, its cross-system and multi-functional characteristics make the controller difficult to achieve coopera-
tive goals. In addition, the chassis system, which has high complexity, numerous subsystems, and strong coupling, 
will also lead to low computing efficiency and poor control effect of the controller. Therefore, this paper proposes 
a scenario-driven hybrid distributed model predictive control algorithm with variable control topology. This algo-
rithm divides multiple stability regions based on the vehicle’s β −γ phase plane, forming a mapping relationship 
between the control structure and the vehicle’s state. A control input fusion mechanism within the transition domain 
is designed to mitigate the problems of system state oscillation and control input jitter caused by switching control 
structures. Then, a distributed state-space equation with state coupling and input coupling characteristics is con-
structed, and a weighted local agent cost function in quadratic programming is derived. Through cost coupling, local 
agents can coordinate global performance goals. Finally, through Simulink/CarSim joint simulation and hardware-in-
the-loop (HIL) test, the proposed algorithm is validated to improve vehicle stability while ensuring trajectory tracking 
accuracy and has good applicability for multi-objective coordinated control. This paper combines the advantages 
of distributed MPC and decentralized MPC, achieving a balance between approximating the global optimal results 
and the solution’s efficiency.
Keywords  Autonomous vehicle, Distributed control, Multi-agent system, Hybrid-DMPC, Variable topology
1  Introduction
With the continuous development of electronic and x-by-
wire technology, active safety functions in vehicle chas-
sis have gradually become indispensable. These functions 
use advanced electronic control systems to monitor the 
vehicle states in real-time and intervene automatically 
when necessary [1], helping drivers control the vehicle 
better and prevent accidents. Chassis active safety func-
tions include active front steering (AFS) [2–4], direct yaw 
moment control (DYC) [5, 6], four-wheel steering (4WS) 
[7–9], and active suspension systems (ASS) [10–12].
AFS is a vehicle steering assistance system that auto-
matically adjusts steering response based on vehicle 
speed and other driving conditions. At low speeds, it pro-
vides quicker steering responses for easier maneuvering, 
while at high speeds, it slows down the steering response 
to prevent oversteering and maintain vehicle stability. 
DYC generates the yaw moment of the car around the 
center of mass by distributing the longitudinal force of

ment helps suppress tendencies of oversteering or under-

4WS allows the front and rear wheels to steer to improve 
the vehicle’s handling and stability. The rear wheels 
can steer in the same or opposite direction to the front 
wheels based on signals such as the front steering angle 
and vehicle speed. ASS can dynamically adjust the stiff-
ness and damping characteristics of the suspension based 
on vehicle states and road conditions. This adaptation 
enhances the vehicle’s handling performance and ride 
comfort under various driving conditions.
The above-mentioned active safety functions acting 
alone on the vehicle can produce better control effects on 
local targets. However, performance targets and control 
inputs often conflict among multiple functions and actu-
ators. For instance, using longitudinal tire force by the 
DYC system can reduce the available lateral force, while 
the 4WS system can influence the DYC’s control over the 
vehicle’s yaw dynamics [13]. Therefore, multi-objective 
coordination across different systems is essential to chas-
sis control. Model Predictive Control (MPC) algorithm 
has been widely applied in the field of chassis cooperative 
control due to its characteristics of rolling optimization, 
feedback correction, and optimal prediction [14, 15]. 
Jing et al. proposed an integrated control strategy based 
on MPC for stability and economy. This strategy uses 
model predictive control to coordinate AFS and DYC, 
achieving low energy consumption of the entire vehicle 
while improving handling stability [16]. Li et al. proposed 
a nonlinear model predictive control-based cooperative 
control algorithm for the four-wheel steering and four-
wheel driving vehicle under extreme conditions, such as 
emergency obstacle avoidance and emergency braking, 
which improved the vehicle’s ability to track multiple 
objectives under extreme states [17]. To enhance vehicle 
handling stability, anti-rollover capability, and ride com-
fort, Wang et al. designed an integrated control strategy 
for longitudinal, lateral, and vertical dynamics of distrib-
uted driving electric vehicles based on particle filtering 
and nonlinear model predictive control [18].
The structure of the MPC algorithm can be divided 
into three categories [19], namely centralized MPC, 
decentralized MPC, and distributed MPC, as shown in 
Figure 1a. The structures used in the above literature are 
all centralized MPC, a traditional control system struc-
ture where all control functions are centralized in a single 
central controller. The central controller is responsible 
for collecting all input data, processing and making deci-
sions, and sending control signals to various actuators. 
The advantage of this architecture is that control is cen-
tralized, which facilitates the overall optimization and 
management of the system [20]. However, its disadvan-
tages are also apparent. The reliability and scalability of 
the system are poor. Once the central controller fails, the 
entire system will become inoperative. In addition, as the 
system scale increases, the central controller’s burden sig-
nificantly increases, leading to performance bottlenecks.
In contrast, decentralized MPC divides control func-
tions among multiple independent controllers. Each

controller does not cause the entire system to paralyze. 
In addition, decentralized MPC can better adapt to the 
system’s expansion needs. However, due to the lack of 
communication between controllers, decentralized MPC 
faces problems that cannot be solved by global optimi-
zation in coordinating complex coupled systems [21]. 
Therefore, it is mainly used in conditions with weak cou-
pling between subsystems and is rarely used in vehicle 
chassis systems. The system usually needs to be decou-
pled first. Li et al. realized the decoupling of longitudinal 
velocity, lateral velocity, and yaw rate through input-
output diagonal decoupling and used an approximate 
decentralized MPC control method to track the vehicle 
trajectory [22]. Chokor et al. established a decentralized 
control architecture and proposed a heuristic solution 
based on decoupled control, using a super-torsion sliding 
mode algorithm to output the values of AFS and DYC. 
Simulation results show that although the decentral-
ized architecture is more robust, it cannot guarantee the 
closed-loop stability of the entire system [23].
In response to the above shortcomings, distributed 
MPC based on multi-agent (MAS) theory has been fur-
ther developed, and the concept of decentralized MPC 
has been improved. As shown in Figure 1c, the system is 
divided into multiple local subsystems, and an independ-
ent controller manages each subsystem. Each control-
ler is responsible for model prediction and optimization 
calculations for its local subsystem and generates local 
control inputs. Meanwhile, information exchange and 
cooperative optimization are carried out between con-
trollers through the network. By sharing local informa-
tion, each controller can achieve global optimal control, 
improving the performance and robustness of the system 
[24, 25]. In addition, distributed MPC can achieve high 
system reliability, and the failure of a single controller 
will not affect the entire system’s operation. This makes 
distributed MPC suitable for large, complex systems that 
require high flexibility and reliability, such as smart grids 
[26], intelligent transportation systems [27], and intel-
ligent manufacturing systems [28]. However, its applica-
tion in vehicle chassis cooperative control is relatively 
rare. Liang et  al. established a cooperative architecture 
composed of AFS agent and DYC agent, forming a state 
equation and global optimization problem with input 
coupling characteristics and optimized control inputs 
through the Pareto optimal theory [29]. Similarly, Liang 
et  al. established AFS agent and ASS agent based on a 
two-degree-of-freedom yaw model and a four-degree-of-
freedom roll model and designed local performance opti-
mization functions with weighting characteristics. Then, 
the optimal solution is obtained through iterative solving 
by exchanging information, and the system’s stability is 
demonstrated [30]. Tang et  al. proposed a wheel-based 
modeling method. Each wheel is an agent and measures 
the contribution of a single agent to the expected total 
moment acting on the center of mass. However, this 
method still requires an upper-level controller responsi-
ble for the calculation of forces/moments [31–33].
Although distributed MPC has the above advantages, 
it requires frequent communication between control-
lers. Furthermore, network delays and communication 
failures can potentially affect system performance. There-
fore, considering the advantages and disadvantages of 
both distributed MPC and decentralized MPC, this paper 
proposes a scenario-driven control topology variable 
algorithm and constructs a hybrid distributed model pre-
dictive control (Hybrid-DMPC) architecture that inte-
grates both algorithm structures. The main contributions 
of this paper are as follows:
(1) An innovative scenario-driven hybrid distributed 
model predictive control algorithm is proposed. This 
algorithm divides the vehicle’s state domain based on 
the β −γ phase plane and forms a mapping relation-
ship between the control structure and the vehicle’s 
state domain. The transition criteria between differ-
ent control structures and control input fusion meth-
ods are designed to prevent system oscillations.
(2) The Steering agent and DYC agent control system 
based on actuator functions are established, and a 
distributed state space equation with state coupling 
and control input coupling characteristics is derived. 
A weighted local agent optimization function con-
sidering cost coupling is designed to coordinate the 
global performance goals of multi-systems.
(3) This paper explains the meaning and transfor-
mation methods of predicted trajectory, assumed 
trajectory, and optimal trajectory, which provides 
a communication basis for information interaction 
between agents. The iterative solution method is 
adopted under the distributed MPC structure, and 
the iterative error is used to balance the solution 
accuracy and efficiency of the controller.
The structure of this paper is as follows. In Section 2, 
a 2-degree-of-freedom control model considering front 
and rear wheel steering and DYC and the Fiala brush 
tire model are established and rewritten into state space

3  Design of Hybrid‑DMPC
As introduced in Section 1, decentralized MPC decom-
poses the entire system into multiple subsystems, with 
no information communication between them. This 
means that each subsystem cannot know the future 
state sequence and control sequence of other subsys-
tems. Therefore, decentralized MPC cannot achieve a 
globally optimal solution under strongly coupled condi-
tions. Distributed MPC retains information exchange 
between controllers while decomposing the entire sys-
tem into multiple subsystems. Through local information 
exchange and collaboration, distributed MPC can achieve 
the global optimal solution equivalent to centralized 
MPC for the whole system. Distributed MPC typically 
has better robustness and scalability because the system’s 
overall performance does not depend on the stability of 
a single controller, and the system’s scale can be adjusted 
by adding or removing control units. However, distrib-
uted MPC also has a higher communication burden.
In addition, vehicle driving scenarios are complex and 
variable, including high-speed cruising, smooth lane 
changes, emergency obstacle avoidance, etc. In these 
scenarios, the control requirements for the controller 
are different. A single control mode or structure can-
not perfectly adapt to all conditions. Therefore, an accu-
rate understanding and effective control of the vehicle’s 
dynamic characteristics are crucial for stability and safety.

3.1  Control Strategy of Weak Stability Domain
When the vehicle is in the weak stability domain, it is 
typically driving at high speed or on a low adhesion sur-
face, and its states may exhibit unpredictable behaviors 
such as severe swaying, loss of control, or even rollover. 
At this time, the tire characteristics deviate from the 
nonlinear region, tire forces approach saturation, and 
the coupling characteristics of lateral and longitudinal 
dynamics are significant. Therefore, the distributed MPC 
control method is used in this region to achieve a global 
optimum solution for the vehicle. The control structure 
at this time is shown in Figure 5a.
In the cooperative control process, information 
exchange is crucial. Different agents exchange infor-
mation with each other via the CAN bus. In addition, 
the vehicle’s states at this moment are also fed back to 
each agent via the CAN bus. The difference is that the 
information exchange between agents includes future 
predictive information, while the feedback information 
from the vehicle only contains the current states and 
control inputs. Based on the above discussion, when 
distributed MPC is used in the weak stability domain, 
each agent only receives the future state sequences and 
control sequences from its neighboring agents. In con-
trast, when decentralized MPC is used in the strong 
stability domain, each agent only receives the feedback 
information from the vehicle.
For distributed MPC, using the state coupling space 
equations established in Section 2.3, a cooperative dis-
tributed model predictive control algorithm is adopted, 
with a cost function selected to achieve global perfor-
mance objectives. Within a single sampling time, an 
iterative update method is used, allowing each agent 
to independently solve its optimization problem and

each agent can only access limited information. A sin-

iterations is crucial. This termination condition should 
be able to ensure control performance while minimiz-

Abstract: The development of chassis active safety control technology has improved vehicle stability under extreme condi- tions. However, its cross-system and multi-functional characteristics make the controller difficult to achieve coopera- tive goals. In addition, the chassis system, which has high complexity, numerous subsystems, and strong coupling, will also lead to low computing efficiency and poor control effect of the controller. Therefore, this paper proposes a scenario-driven hybrid distributed model predictive control algorithm with variable control topology. This algo- rithm divides multiple stability regions based on the vehicle’s β −γ phase plane, forming a mapping relationship between the control structure and the vehicle’s state. A control input fusion mechanism within the transition domain is designed to mitigate the problems of system state oscillation and control input jitter caused by switching control structures. Then, a distributed state-space equation with state coupling and input coupling characteristics is con- structed, and a weighted local agent cost function in quadratic programming is derived. Through cost coupling, local agents can coordinate global performance goals. Finally, through Simulink/CarSim joint simulation and hardware-in- the-loop (HIL) test, the proposed algorithm is validated to improve vehicle stability while ensuring trajectory tracking accuracy and has good applicability for multi-objective coordinated control. This paper combines the advantages of distributed MPC and decentralized MPC, achieving a balance between approximating the global optimal results and the solution’s efficiency.
